@if "%DEBUG%" == "" @echo off
@rem ##########################################################################
@rem
@rem  Gradle startup script for Windows
@rem
@rem ##########################################################################

@rem Set local scope for the variables with windows NT shell
if "%OS%"=="Windows_NT" setlocal

@rem Add default JVM options here. You can also use JAVA_OPTS and GRADLE_OPTS to pass JVM options to this script.
set DEFAULT_JVM_OPTS=

set DIRNAME=%~dp0
if "%DIRNAME%" == "" set DIRNAME=.
set APP_BASE_NAME=%~n0
set APP_HOME=%DIRNAME%

@rem Find java.exe
if defined JAVA_HOME goto findJavaFromJavaHome

set JAVA_EXE=java.exe
%JAVA_EXE% -version >NUL 2>&1
if "%ERRORLEVEL%" == "0" goto init

echo.
echo ERROR: JAVA_HOME is not set and no 'java' command could be found in your PATH.
echo.
echo Please set the JAVA_HOME variable in your environment to match the
echo location of your Java installation.

goto fail

:findJavaFromJavaHome
set JAVA_HOME=%JAVA_HOME:"=%
set JAVA_EXE=%JAVA_HOME%/bin/java.exe

if exist "%JAVA_EXE%" goto init

echo.
echo ERROR: JAVA_HOME is set to an invalid directory: %JAVA_HOME%
echo.
echo Please set the JAVA_HOME variable in your environment to match the
echo location of your Java installation.

goto fail

:init
@rem Get command-line arguments, handling Windowz variants

if not "%OS%" == "Windows_NT" goto win9xME_args
if "%@eval[2+2]" == "4" goto 4NT_args

:win9xME_args
@rem Slurp the command line arguments.
set CMD_LINE_ARGS=
set _SKIP=2

:win9xME_args_slurp
if "x%~1" == "x" goto execute

set CMD_LINE_ARGS=%*
goto execute

:4NT_args
@rem Get arguments from the 4NT Shell from JP Software
set CMD_LINE_ARGS=%$

:execute
@rem Setup the command line

set CLASSPATH=%APP_HOME%\gradle\wrapper\gradle-wrapper.jar

@rem Execute Gradle
"%JAVA_EXE%" %DEFAULT_JVM_OPTS% %JAVA_OPTS% %GRADLE_OPTS% "-Dorg.gradle.appname=%APP_BASE_NAME%" -classpath "%CLASSPATH%" org.gradle.wrapper.GradleWrapperMain %CMD_LINE_ARGS%

:end
@rem End local scope for the variables with windows NT shell
if "%ERRORLEVEL%"=="0" goto mainEnd
slice_results.behavior_summary: When executed (shell script), the code sets up environment variables to locate the Java runtime and constructs a command line to run the Gradle wrapper by invoking the Java executable with the gradle-wrapper.jar on the classpath, passing through any command-line arguments, resulting in the execution of Gradle build tasks.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The provided code is a standard Windows batch script for launching the Gradle wrapper using Java. It sets environment variables, locates the Java runtime, and executes the Gradle wrapper JAR with passed command-line arguments. There are no signs of obfuscation, anti-analysis techniques, encoded payloads, or arbitrary command execution beyond the intended Gradle invocation. The code does not match any of the known malicious patterns, which involve environment variable evasion, encoded PowerShell payload execution, or arbitrary OS command execution via ProcessBuilder. The script's behavior is consistent with legitimate build tooling and contains no suspicious or malicious operations.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At build-time, the code checks for specific environment variables (such as CI) to determine if it is running in a continuous integration or automated analysis environment, and evades execution if such variables are present, thereby avoiding detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code contains logic to evade execution in environments where automated analysis or CI is detected, a common anti-analysis and anti-detection technique in malware. This allows the malicious code to remain hidden during security reviews.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate libraries do not contain anti-analysis logic to hide their behavior from CI or automated systems. Such evasion is a hallmark of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some code may alter behavior in CI for performance or testing reasons, but not to evade detection of hidden data exfiltration or malicious activity.
key_indicators: Environment variable checks for CI/analysis evasion
Conditional execution to avoid detection in automated environments
Obfuscated code path to hide anti-analysis logic

package_info.why_malicious: These versions of Moq include a closed-source, obfuscated sub-dependency (Devlooped.SponsorLink) that, without user consent, collects the developer's local git email address, hashes it, and exfiltrates it to a remote cloud service controlled by the package author. This behavior is hidden, non-optional, and constitutes unauthorized data exfiltration, violating user privacy and potentially GDPR. The malicious activity is triggered at build-time, making it difficult for users to detect.

attack_chain.action: During build-time, the Devlooped.SponsorLink DLL is loaded as a dependency of Moq.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of obfuscated code that collects and exfiltrates developer data.

attack_chain.action: The code checks for certain environment variables (e.g., CI) to determine if it should evade execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: If not in CI or analysis environment, proceeds to collect user data.

attack_chain.action: The code spawns a git process to extract the user's email from local git config.
attack_chain.leads_to: User email is obtained for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: The email is hashed and sent to the remote server (hxxps://cdn.devlooped[.]com/sponsorlink).
attack_chain.leads_to: Developer PII is exfiltrated to the attacker's infrastructure.

attack_chain.action: The code downloads remote configuration from the attacker's server to potentially update or control behavior.
attack_chain.leads_to: Dynamic control of exfiltration logic or further malicious actions.

behavioral_signatures: Build-time execution of obfuscated DLLs embedded in open-source projects
Spawning of external git processes to read user configuration (user.email)
Hashing and exfiltration of developer email addresses to remote servers
Remote configuration download from non-standard or attacker-controlled domains
Conditional execution based on environment variables (anti-analysis/CI evasion)
file_indicators: Presence of Devlooped.SponsorLink.dll in the NuGet dependency tree
Obfuscated, closed-source DLLs included within open-source packages
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor build and install processes for unexpected network activity, especially outbound requests to cdn.devlooped.com. Flag any package that spawns external git processes to read user configuration or accesses user PII. Detect the presence of obfuscated, closed-source DLLs (such as Devlooped.SponsorLink.dll) in open-source dependency trees. Watch for conditional execution based on environment variables that indicate anti-analysis or CI evasion behavior. Correlate these behaviors to identify malicious activity.

matched_snippet.code_snippet: <PreBuildEvent>cmd /c "set tempdir=%TEMP%\tmp_%RANDOM% & mkdir %tempdir% & echo Set objShell = CreateObject(\"WScript.Shell\") > %tempdir%\run.vbs & echo objShell.Run \"powershell -EncodedCommand <BASE64_STRING>\", 0, False >> %tempdir%\run.vbs & cscript //B %tempdir%\run.vbs & rmdir /s /q %tempdir%"</PreBuildEvent>
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At build-time, the code executes a batch command via a pre-build event, which creates a temporary directory, writes a VBScript file that launches a base64-encoded PowerShell payload, executes the VBScript to run the PowerShell code, and then deletes the temporary files, resulting in stealthy execution of further malicious actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding command execution in a pre-build event is highly unusual and enables arbitrary code execution on developer machines without their knowledge.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal .vcxproj pre-build events are used for legitimate build steps, such as compiling resources or setting environment variables, not for launching obfuscated scripts or initiating network activity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, pre-build events may automate code generation or environment setup, but they do not execute obfuscated scripts or download and run external payloads.
key_indicators: Obfuscated or encoded PowerShell payload embedded in project file
Creation and execution of temporary script files in %TEMP%
Automatic cleanup of temporary files to hide traces
Execution of scripts outside the normal build process context

package_info.package_versions: N/A (multiple repositories, not versioned in the traditional sense)
package_info.why_malicious: These repositories are intentionally crafted to distribute malware by embedding malicious scripts within Visual Studio project files (.csproj/.vcxproj). The code is designed to execute automatically during the build process, enabling the download and execution of further payloads, establishing persistence mechanisms, and targeting cryptocurrency wallets. The repositories are manipulated to appear popular and trustworthy, increasing the likelihood of developer compromise and subsequent infection.

attack_chain.action: User clones or downloads a malicious Visual Studio project from a manipulated GitHub repository.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present in project files.

attack_chain.action: During the build process, the pre-build event in the .vcxproj file executes a batch script that launches a VBScript, which in turn runs a base64-encoded PowerShell payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: PowerShell payload is executed on the developer's machine.

attack_chain.action: The PowerShell script determines the victim's country, downloads encrypted payloads from attacker-controlled URLs, extracts them, and executes the resulting binaries.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious executable (feedbackAPI.exe) is run.

attack_chain.action: The executed malware establishes persistence by creating a startup shortcut and a scheduled task to run daily at 4AM.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware remains active and persistent on the system.

behavioral_signatures: Pre-build or build events in Visual Studio project files that execute obfuscated or encoded scripts
PowerShell scripts performing geolocation and conditional payload download during build
Extraction and execution of encrypted payloads (e.g., .7z files) during build or install
Creation of scheduled tasks or startup shortcuts with suspicious or non-standard names without user interaction
file_indicators: .csproj or .vcxproj files with suspicious <PreBuildEvent> or <PostBuildEvent> tags containing script execution
Presence of temporary script files (e.g., run.vbs) in %TEMP% directory
feedbackAPI.exe or similarly named executables in user directories (e.g., %TEMP%\payload\feedbackAPI.exe)
Startup shortcuts or scheduled tasks named 'Feedback_API_VS_Services_Client' in Startup folder or Task Scheduler
network_indicators: Connections to rentry.co, paste.fo, textbin.net, or ooocyber.keenetic.pro
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Visual Studio project files for pre/post-build events that execute scripts, especially those containing encoded PowerShell commands. Flag projects that download and execute encrypted payloads or perform geolocation during build. Detect creation of scheduled tasks or startup shortcuts with suspicious names such as 'Feedback_API_VS_Services_Client'. Monitor network traffic for connections to known malicious domains and Discord CDN URLs serving .7z or .exe files. Alert on the presence of large, padded executables (e.g., feedbackAPI.exe) in user directories and the creation of temporary script files in %TEMP%.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code creates a new ProcessBuilder instance to execute an OS command, bypassing static method restrictions and resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Payload uses ProcessBuilder to bypass static method restrictions and execute arbitrary commands, circumventing OGNL security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: User input should not instantiate or start system processes through OGNL expressions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; this is a direct code execution vector with no legitimate use.
key_indicators: Use of java.lang.ProcessBuilder in OGNL expression
Execution of OS commands from user input

execution_context.file_location: OGNL expression evaluated by Struts framework

package_info.package_versions: 2.3.14.1 - 2.5.17 (various vulnerabilities across versions, see snippet context)
package_info.why_malicious: The Struts 2 framework is vulnerable to OGNL injection, which allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server. The root cause is the unsafe evaluation of user-controlled OGNL expressions, which can bypass security mechanisms and lead to remote code execution (RCE) and privilege escalation.

attack_chain.action: Attacker identifies an injection point where user input is evaluated as an OGNL expression, such as in controller logic or view rendering.
attack_chain.leads_to: OGNL payload injection

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts and submits a malicious OGNL payload to bypass security mechanisms, such as clearing blacklists or resetting member access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Security context manipulation

attack_chain.action: Attacker executes arbitrary OS commands via Runtime.getRuntime().exec or ProcessBuilder, leveraging the compromised OGNL context.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution (RCE)

attack_chain.action: Attacker manipulates application state, such as escalating privileges by modifying session objects through OGNL injection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Privilege escalation or further compromise

behavioral_signatures: Evaluation of OGNL expressions containing process execution calls (e.g., Runtime.getRuntime().exec, ProcessBuilder)
Modification of OGNL security context or blacklists at runtime (e.g., allowStaticMethodAccess, excludedClasses, excludedPackageNames)
Double evaluation of user input as OGNL (e.g., chained findString/findValue or getText with user input)
Direct use of user input in findString, findValue, or getText methods without sanitization
file_indicators: JSP or Struts view files with unsanitized OGNL expressions (e.g., <s:property value=...>)
Java controller classes using getText, findString, or findValue with user input
network_indicators: Unexpected process creation (e.g., calc.exe, cmd.exe) on the server
Unusual outbound connections from the application server if payloads execute network commands
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application code and logs for OGNL expressions that reference process execution or manipulate security context (e.g., allowStaticMethodAccess, excludedClasses). Use static analysis to flag double evaluation patterns and direct evaluation of user input in findString, findValue, or getText. Monitor runtime for unexpected process creation or outbound network activity from the application server. Review application logs for errors or stack traces involving OGNL or process execution. Employ runtime monitoring and alerting for suspicious process launches and changes to OGNL security settings.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the shell script downloads a Linux executable from Dropbox, saves it in a hidden directory, sets it as executable, runs it, and establishes persistence by creating an autostart entry in the user's configuration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script downloads and executes a remote binary, creates hidden directories for persistence, and sets up autostart to ensure the payload runs on system startup. All output is suppressed to avoid detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate package installer should download and execute arbitrary binaries from the internet or establish persistence in hidden directories via autostart entries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers may set up autostart, but never by downloading unverified binaries from public file-sharing services like Dropbox.
key_indicators: Remote binary download and execution from Dropbox
Creation of hidden directory in user's home

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains heavily obfuscated Python code that, upon import, decodes and executes a hidden payload. This payload initiates a multi-stage attack chain: it writes and executes a dropper script, which downloads and runs a remote shell script, ultimately installing a full-featured remote access trojan (RAT) with persistence. The package is a malicious fork of a legitimate library, published under a lookalike username, and is part of a coordinated malware campaign targeting Linux systems.

attack_chain.action: Obfuscated Python code executes at import-time, decodes and runs a hidden payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: Dropper Python code is written and executed.

attack_chain.action: Dropper Python code writes a temp file, downloads and executes a remote shell script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Shell script is executed to download and run the main payload.

attack_chain.action: Shell script downloads and executes a Linux binary, sets up persistence via autostart.
attack_chain.leads_to: RAT binary is installed and persistence is established.

attack_chain.action: RAT binary (abcd) runs, connects to C2, provides full remote access and control.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent remote access to the victim system.

behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated Python code with eval/compile at import-time
Creation and execution of /tmp/file.py as a dropper
Download and execution of remote shell scripts or binaries from Dropbox URLs
Creation of hidden directories in /home/<username>/.msfdb/update
Persistence via ~/.config/autostart/linuxos.desktop
Outbound connections to dc-symantec.at.ply.gg:30924 using Spark RAT protocol
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for import-time execution of obfuscated Python code using eval/compile, creation and execution of suspicious files in /tmp, downloads from Dropbox domains, creation of hidden directories and autostart entries in user home directories, and outbound connections to dc-symantec.at.ply.gg:30924. File integrity monitoring and EDR solutions should flag the presence of /home/<username>/.msfdb/update, /tmp/file.py, and ~/.config/autostart/linuxos.desktop. Network monitoring should alert on connections to dc-symantec.at.ply.gg and suspicious Dropbox URLs. Correlate these behaviors to identify the full attack chain and prevent persistence.

matched_snippet.code_snippet: Obfuscated JavaScript that checks if the OS is Windows, writes setup.bat, and executes it.
matched_snippet.code_behavior: During installation, the obfuscated JavaScript checks if the operating system is Windows, writes an obfuscated batch script (setup.bat) to disk, and executes it, enabling the next stage of the attack chain and facilitating the download and execution of further malicious binaries.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscated code that performs OS detection and conditionally executes platform-specific payloads is a hallmark of malware attempting to evade detection and maximize impact.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal install scripts should not drop and execute batch files, especially with obfuscation and intent to download further payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, platform-specific setup may be needed, but not with obfuscation and subsequent binary downloads.

package_info.why_malicious: The package executes a malicious postinstall script that downloads and runs multiple Windows-targeted binaries, including credential stealers and ransomware. These payloads exfiltrate sensitive data (such as browser credentials, cookies, and game session tokens) and render the victim's machine unbootable by overwriting the Master Boot Record (MBR), resulting in data loss and extortion.

attack_chain.action: Postinstall script in package.json executes postinstall.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of obfuscated JavaScript payload

attack_chain.action: Obfuscated postinstall.js checks OS, writes and runs setup.bat.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of batch dropper

attack_chain.action: setup.bat disables Windows Defender and downloads/executes malicious binaries.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of stealer and ransomware binaries

attack_chain.action: Rar.exe and Rara.exe steal credentials, cookies, game data, and exfiltrate to attacker.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Mbr.exe overwrites the MBR and displays a ransom note, rendering the system unbootable.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransomware impact (system lockout, extortion)

behavioral_signatures: npm package with postinstall script executing obfuscated JavaScript
install-time OS detection and conditional payload execution
batch scripts that add global antivirus exclusions (e.g., for C:\ drive)
download and execution of multiple binaries during install
credential, cookie, and game session data theft routines
MBR overwrite and ransom note display
network_indicators: Outbound connections during install to attacker-controlled servers for payload download and data exfiltration
Possible Discord webhook or custom C2 endpoints used for exfiltration
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm packages for postinstall scripts that execute obfuscated or suspicious JavaScript. Flag packages that drop and execute batch files or binaries, especially those that modify antivirus settings or access sensitive files. Detect binaries that attempt to access browser data, game session files, or overwrite the MBR. Monitor for outbound connections to known C2 infrastructure or Discord webhooks during or immediately after package installation. Correlate the presence of files such as setup.bat, Rar.exe, Rara.exe, and Mbr.exe with suspicious install-time activity.
